newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Aleman announces fiscal austerity in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Aleman announces fiscal austerity in Nicaragua.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman on Monday announced tough public spending austerity measures designed to bring economic stability to his impoverished Central American country.

The austerity measures, which Aleman described as "serious and drastic," will hold 1997 government spending to its 1996 level of 2.25 billion cordobas ($249 million) -- a decrease of about 10 percent in real terms -- and freeze government hiring.

As he symbolically cut up credit cards before photographers, Aleman said the government would tighten its own belt, too -- eliminating the use of government credit cards and most government cars, cellular telephones and spending accounts.
Central Bank President Noel Ramirez told Reuters the moves will save Nicaragua about 500 or 600 million cordobas ($55 million to $66 million) a year.

Ramirez said the austerity measures will help the government reduce inflation, which stood at 12 percent in 1996, and free up resources to help boost production, especially agricultural production in the private sector.
Aleman, the right-wing former lawyer, took power on Jan. 10 promising to streamline the bloated state payroll in Nicaragua, which had a Marxist government from 1979 to 1990.
But Monday he said that while he had frozen government hiring, he would not be firing state workers given that more than 50 percent of Nicaragua's work force was unemployed or underemployed.
"Fiscal austerity does not mean we throw public employees on the street, only that people should look for different ways to live, not through the enormous state apparatus," Aleman said.

The Nicaraguan economy has grown for three consecutive years after a decade of economic hardship, including 5.5 percent growth in 1996. But despite the growth, unemployment and poverty have remained high.
